summary: Mobbin reviewed 2,108 dashboards and argues that the basics (clear hierarchy, good spacing, useful charts) make a dashboard fine but not memorable. The dashboards that stick are one step ahead: they put key insights and next steps next to the data, package stats into recaps and highlights, and pick visuals that make the data make sense instantly, such as a real-time view where every dot is a real visitor, a heat map, or a clean layout when most dashboards look busy. On mobile, standout dashboards turn personal data into shareable formats like a swipeable story, and some products coin their own metric (streaks, a readiness score, closing rings) that keeps users loyal. AI is filling the 'why did this change?' gap, from a single prompt under a chart to a full AI layer beside the data. For a design system, it gives a dashboard stance: design for understanding and next action, leave things out, and test each screen with the question 'Would I screenshot this, and why?'
key_ideas: Clear hierarchy, good spacing and useful charts make a dashboard fine, but not memorable.
Memorable dashboards are one step ahead: they show what to do about the data, not only what happened.
Key insights placed next to a chart turn a plain line chart into guidance.
Recaps, daily briefs and post-activity highlights package data so it is easy to understand and feels like an accomplishment.
Standout dashboards pick visuals that fit the data, such as a real-time view where every dot is a real visitor or a heat map where darker means busier.
Most dashboards look busy, so a very clean one stands out.
Small moments of delight, like a cake inside a donut chart or a game instead of an empty table, show the dashboard was not a template.
The word dashboard began as a carriage's mud board and became the place for signals in cars; the form keeps changing, but the job never changed.
When products do roughly the same thing, the dashboard does a lot of the convincing: it shows what the product does, how you are doing and what to do next.
On mobile, data can be presented like content, for example a swipeable story that people want to share.
Coining your own metric (streaks, readiness score, closing rings) makes the metric part of how users talk and makes switching unlikely.
AI is filling the gap of explaining why a number changed, from a single prompt below a chart to a full AI layer beside the data.
The author's gut check for a dashboard is: would I screenshot this, and why?
The dashboards worth screenshotting were not the prettiest; they knew what to leave out.

rules.rule: Place key insights next to a chart instead of showing the chart alone.
rules.why: A chart alone shows what happened; insights beside it show what to do about it.
rules.evidence: [0:50] Instead of just a line chart, Faith puts the key insights

rules.rule: Make the dashboard show what the product does, how the user is doing and what to do next, not only report numbers.
rules.why: One screenshot should tell you what the product does, how you're doing, and what to do next; the dashboard does a lot of the convincing when products are similar.
rules.evidence: [2:50] One screenshot that tells you exactly what this product does

rules.rule: Choose each visualization by asking how to make this data make sense to your users instantly, rather than dropping in a template chart.
rules.why: The standout dashboards clearly weren't templates; someone thought about how users would get the data instantly.
rules.evidence: [1:59] You can tell these weren't templates

rules.rule: Decide what to leave out of a dashboard; prefer a clean layout over a busy one.
rules.why: Most dashboards look busy, so a clean one stands out, and the dashboards worth screenshotting knew what to leave out.
rules.evidence: [4:39] They were the ones that knew what to leave out

rules.rule: Check each dashboard screen with the question 'Would I screenshot this, and why?'
rules.why: The author keeps going back to it after thousands of dashboards; the ones worth screenshotting weren't the prettiest but knew what to leave out.
rules.evidence: [4:30] going back to that one simple gut check

rules.rule: Package activity stats into highlights, recaps or a daily brief instead of raw numbers.
rules.why: Runner's post-run highlights give a sense of accomplishment; Origin's weekly recap is easy to understand.
rules.evidence: [1:09] Runner packages your stats into highlights

rules.rule: In a heat map, use darker squares to mean more activity.
rules.why: Front's heat map reads at a glance because darker squares just mean busier hours.
rules.evidence: [1:40] darker squares just mean busier hours

rules.rule: Consider showing live activity as individual marks, where every dot is a real person active right now.
rules.why: Shopify's Live View lets you monitor store visitors in real time, where every dot is a real person browsing right now; it stands out from dashboards that look the same.
rules.evidence: [1:25] across the globe in real time

rules.rule: When the user has cleared everything, show something rewarding instead of an empty table.
rules.why: Mercury lets you play a game after you've paid all your bills, one of the signs the dashboard was not a template.
rules.evidence: [1:52] Instead of showing an empty table

rules.rule: Consider a playful touch tied to what the data means, such as a birthday cake inside an ownership donut chart.
rules.why: Cake's donut chart is one of the examples that show the dashboard was not a template.
rules.evidence: [1:46] put a literal birthday cake inside their ownership donut chart

rules.rule: On mobile, consider presenting personal data as swipeable story-like content.
rules.why: Opal's story format lets you swipe through your own data like content, and when it looks this good people share it.
rules.evidence: [3:02] Opal turns screen time insights into a format like Instagram story

rules.rule: Consider coining a product-specific metric that users can adopt in their own words.
rules.why: Streaks, a readiness score and closing rings become how users talk about what they did, and once that happens a user is very unlikely to switch to another fitness tracker.
rules.evidence: [3:23] some products start coining their own

rules.rule: Offer AI help to answer why a number changed, either as a prompt right below the chart or as an AI layer alongside the data.
rules.why: Users stare at dashboards asking what changed or caused a spike; AI is filling that gap.

decisions.question: Should the dashboard show only the data, or also tell people what it means and what to do?

options.name: Data only
options.effect: A chart shows what happened; the dashboard works but is easy to forget.
options.when: The source does not recommend it; it describes most dashboards this way.

options.name: Insights next to the chart
options.effect: Key insights sit beside the line chart and show what to do about it (Faith).
options.when: When users need to act on the data.

options.name: Recaps and briefs
options.effect: A weekly recap and a daily brief package the data so it is easy to understand (Origin); post-activity highlights give a sense of accomplishment (Runner).
options.when: When data accumulates over time or after an activity.

decisions.recommendation: Go one step ahead of the data: show what to do about it, not only what happened, because those are the dashboards people remember.
decisions.evidence: [0:48] The ones I kept coming back to, they're always one step ahead

decisions.question: How should the dashboard look so it stands out instead of looking like a template?

options.name: Standard busy dashboard
options.effect: Clear hierarchy, spacing and charts; fine but forgettable, and most dashboards look busy.
options.when: The source presents this as the default it wants to move past.

options.name: Very clean layout
options.effect: A clean layout that stands out because most dashboards look busy (Visitors).
options.when: When the core data is simple enough to show calmly [inferred].

options.name: Data-fitted visualization
options.effect: A visual that matches the data, like a real-time view where every dot is a real visitor (Shopify Live View) or a heat map where darker means busier (Front).
options.when: When a specific visual makes the data make sense instantly.

options.name: Moment of delight
options.effect: A playful touch, like a birthday cake inside an ownership donut chart (Cake) or a game instead of an empty table (Mercury).
options.when: When the product has room for personality [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Design the visual around how users will understand the data instantly, and know what to leave out; the author's gut check is whether you would screenshot it.

decisions.question: What should the screen show when the user has cleared everything, such as all bills paid?

options.name: Empty table
options.effect: An empty table remains after the work is done.
options.when: The source uses it as the contrast case.

options.name: A reward or game
options.effect: The user gets to play a game instead of seeing an empty table (Mercury).
options.when: When finishing everything is an achievement worth marking [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: The source holds up Mercury's game as a non-template choice over an empty table.
decisions.evidence: [1:52] Instead of showing an empty table after you've paid all your bills

decisions.question: Should the product report standard measures, or coin a metric of its own?

options.name: Standard metrics
options.effect: Users describe results in generic terms, like working out for 30 minutes.
options.when: When the product has no signature behaviour to name [inferred].

options.name: Coined metric
options.effect: A named measure like streaks (Duolingo), a readiness score (Oura) or closing rings (Apple) enters how users talk.
options.when: When you want the measure to enter how users talk and keep them from switching.

decisions.recommendation: The source highlights coined metrics: once a user says 'I closed my rings', they are very unlikely to switch fitness trackers.
decisions.evidence: [3:23] some products start coining their own

decisions.question: How much AI should sit on the dashboard to explain why the data changed?

options.name: None
options.effect: Users are left asking what changed or caused a spike.
options.when: The source does not state when [inferred].

options.name: A single prompt below the chart
options.effect: A subtle entry point right under the chart for asking about the data.
options.when: When a light touch is enough [inferred].

options.name: A full AI layer
options.effect: An AI you can talk to right alongside your data.
options.when: When users need deeper explanation of their data [inferred].

decisions.evidence: [3:55] Sometimes as subtle as a single prompt right below your chart

process.detail: Get clear hierarchy, good spacing and useful charts in place; they make a dashboard fine but not memorable.

process.step: Ask how users will get it
process.detail: For each piece of data, ask how to make it make sense to your users so they get it instantly, instead of using a template.
Show how the user is doing and what to do next, for example insights beside a chart, a recap, a brief or highlights.
Remove what does not help; the dashboards worth screenshotting knew what to leave out.
Ask 'Would I screenshot this, and why?' before calling the dashboard done.

caveats: Published by Mobbin, whose library is the data source; the video promotes Mobbin and its statistics (daily searches, one in five home screens, AI dashboards' saves and exports) are platform data that cannot be checked from the video.
Ends with a plug for Mobbin's onboarding-flow video and an upcoming paywalls video, plus a subscribe request.
Auto-generated captions with [music] markers; some product names (Faith, Runner, Visitors, Orbit) are as captioned and may be misheard.
The patterns are the author's opinion from browsing screenshots, not measured outcomes; the only usage number is Mobbin saves and exports, which shows what designers collect, not what users prefer.
The claim that coined metrics make switching very unlikely is stated as an assertion without data.
Published 2026-05-05; the AI dashboard trend reflects that moment.
The process steps are assembled from separate points in the video; the video gives no ordered method, so the order is [inferred].
